Title: Shhh! Whatever you do, don't center the murderous extremists
Article_Text:
Daniel Winston is an American-Israeli therapist, lecturer and author. He volunteers in the IDF reserves, as an MDA medic, in ZAKA, and in the Israel Police Search and Rescue Team.
Twenty-five years after nineteen Muslim terrorists murdered three thousand Americans in the name of a specific, published, endlessly reiterated religious ideology of violent global conquest, the largest school district in Virginia handed its teachers a six-page document instructing them not to bring it up. Fairfax County Public Schools tells educators not to "associate the 9/11 attacks with Islam or Muslims," and not to "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists." It never names Osama bin Laden. It never names Khalid Sheikh Mohammed. It contains roughly thirty references to Islam, anti-Muslim racism and Islamophobic rhetoric, and spends perhaps fifteen percent of its length on the events of that bloody day.
A retired vice admiral who was inside the Pentagon when the plane came through the wall called the guide vanilla. He was being oddly polite about a cowardice that any society that wants to live should be confronting far more forcefully.
Virginia went further. A 2021 Department of Education webinar for teachers, produced under a Democratic governor, instructed them to describe September 11 as a foreign attack by extremists, advised that naming the hijackers was not a relevant detail, and opened from the premise that there is no Muslim responsibility to examine. Glenn Youngkin's administration took it down. This spring the General Assembly put it back and Governor Spanberger signed the bill. A legislature convened, debated, voted, and enacted into law the restoration of a training video whose pedagogical core is that American schoolchildren should not be told who attacked them or why. Not a rogue consultant. Not a viral lesson plan. A statute mandating vagueness.
The material filling the vacuum nationally is of a piece.
"Teaching Beyond September 11th," developed at the University of Pennsylvania's Graduate School of Education and recommended by the education departments of Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Wisconsin and Oregon, gives the attacks themselves a single paragraph. It counts the nineteen hijackers among the dead, as though they had been passengers. It cannot bring itself to use the word "terrorist," and reports that the United States "accused" bin Laden of masterminding the plot, converting a man's own filmed confessions into an allegation the Americans generated from their gut.
New York City's education department spent more than a million dollars over fourteen years on teacher training built around the putative issue of post-9/11 Islamophobia. Only two states, Arizona and Florida, require that the attack be taught at all.
This is not squeamishness. What is being taught is a positive doctrine of radical leftist indoctrination: that inquiry into the enemy's identity, religious ideology, and openly stated reasons is itself the moral offense. Not inaccurate. Not unkind. Offensive, in the technical sense that it constitutes an unfair act of aggression against a protected party which endangers innocent Muslims. Once you accept that premise, everything downstream follows with perfect and enervating logic:
You cannot name him. You cannot quote him. You cannot ask what he believed, because the asking is the true crime, and the child who asks must be redirected before he gets an answer. America's slavish devotion to "conversation" has reached peak suicidality: a civilization that has decided naming your enemy and his religion is impolite or triggering - while your enemy remains entirely unembarrassed about naming you, and worse.
None of this was improvised in a curriculum office in 2021, and the pedigree is not a secret. In 1965 Herbert Marcuse argued that even-handed tolerance is a fraud, because giving every position the same hearing preserves whichever position already holds power. His remedy was tolerance with a thumb on the scale, withdrawn from the right and extended to the left, on the grounds that suppression in the service of justice and liberation is not suppression at all.
Six years later he wrote to the German radical Rudi Dutschke endorsing what Dutschke had christened the long march through the institutions, and spelled out the method: occupy the institutions, work against them from inside them, build counterinstitutions within their walls. Underneath both sits Antonio Gramsci, who understood that a free society is taken trench by trench, through the schools and presses that manufacture what a people takes for granted. A district guide telling teachers to disrupt colleagues who use the wrong vocabulary is not an innovation. It is that essay as a radically visionary lesson plan, written by educators who have never heard the name Marcuse. A doctrine has fully arrived only when the people executing it experience it and brand it as simple decency.
And this is why the people cheering for killers are not a separate phenomenon. The examples here are Islamic, but the rot is more pervasive, and it bears fruit wherever it is planted. Brian Thompson was shot in the back on a Manhattan sidewalk and within days a substantial number of young Americans had located the real story in the claims-denial rate of a health insurer.
Luigi Mangione became a folk hero to people who have never disputed that he pulled the trigger, which is the point.
Charlie Kirk was shot through the neck in front of a crowd and the discourse turned, almost without pausing for breath, to an audit of his opinions.
The murdered men were demoted from subject to setting, a stage on which systemic grievance could be examined by self-ordained justice warriors. That is the identical move Fairfax makes. Do not center the known perpetrator - completely and intentionally regardless of his perfidy. Center the conditions. The only difference is that one produces a fandom and the other a lesson plan, and the lesson plan came first and cuts deeper.
The multi-generational, pan-cultural carriers of this bug are not mysterious. The teachers unions sit astride the pipeline and have made activism in the name of justice the organizing purpose of professional development, and the National Education Association's own 9/11 material has reached for Edward Said, who located the cause of the attacks in American support for the Jewish state.
Academia supplies the theory and launders it into credentials. A press staffed almost entirely by that academy's graduates ratifies it, so that a child taught not to center the extremists meets, at twenty-four, a news environment confirming he was taught correctly. If I were feeling generous I would say none of them are radical ideologues at all, only professionals who grasped long ago that persuading a population does not begin with an election. It begins in kindergarten, it takes twenty years, and they were willing to wait. The generosity makes the picture worse, because a conviction can be argued with and a long con cannot, and by the time it comes to fruition the inversion will be irreversible.
A society taught from childhood to withhold judgment retains no instrument with which to correct or defend itself. It does not collapse. It rots from the inside out, on schedule, until the unnameable enemy need only stroll in and take what is no longer defended.
Soft moral relativism of yesteryear was always destined to shift to hard moral inversion. It could not have ended anywhere else. If no framework may be ranked above another, judgment itself becomes the sole available sin, and the only people left who can be judged are the ones still doing the judging. The murderer has a context. The victim has, at best, a begrudging mention.
The teacher who says plainly that nineteen men murdered three thousand civilians because they believed Allah and Islam required it has committed the one unforgivable act, which is to have asserted something. The doctrine never produces symmetry. Nobody is told to avoid centering the extremist when he is a white nationalist, and nobody should be. The protection runs one direction, which tells you it was never a principle about violence. It was a principle about power, and about shaping America's next cohort of teachers and voters until the subversion is self-perpetuating and permanent.
Asra Nomani, the American Muslim journalist who obtained the Fairfax guide, said she was disturbed by the attempt to convert Muslim students into the primary victims of 9/11. She understands what the authors of these curricula do not: a faith is not honored by being placed beyond query and conclusion. It is infantilized. The nineteen told us who they were, in writing, at length, in advance and afterward.
We have spent twenty-five years and a great deal of public money building an apparatus whose central function is to guarantee that no American child ever finds out who perpetrated 9/11. They are not confused about us. We have proudly made a curriculum out of being confused about them, and continue to do so at our own peril.

Title: Sheeran has not commented publicly since losing the artists' support
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran to return to stage for 1st time since Macklemore was cut, other acts withdrew
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour Saturday — possibly solo — after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.
It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.
Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.
Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists’ support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday’s show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations plans to protest outside the show Saturday afternoon.
The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.
Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran’s representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.
Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.
Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.
The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn’t be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.
He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran’s magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

Title: U.S. Chamber Endorses Rep. Ryan Mackenzie for Pennsylvania's Seventh District During National Bus Tour
Article_Text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce announced its endorsement of Rep. Ryan Mackenzie for Pennsylvania's Seventh District. The event was a stop on the Chamber’s Opportunity Tour, a six-week national bus tour promoting free enterprise.
The U.S. Chamber endorses candidates for federal office who will support policies that drive innovation, grow the economy, and create opportunities for American businesses and workers.
“The U.S. Chamber is proud to endorse Rep. Ryan Mackenzie for reelection to represent Pennsylvania’s seventh district. Throughout his first term in Congress, Ryan has been a strong advocate for pro-growth, free enterprise policies that positively impact Pennsylvanians. He is committed to addressing affordability, protecting taxpayers, growing the economy, and creating opportunities for local businesses and workers to thrive. We are proud to stand beside him in Allentown today, and we look forward to continuing to work with him next Congress,” said Neil Bradley, Executive Vice President and Chief Policy Officer at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
The Opportunity Tour is a part of the U.S. Chamber’s New Fight for Free Enterprise initiative, a multi-year strategic effort to defend, protect, and promote free enterprise.
For six weeks, the Free Enterprise Express bus will visit the businesses whose ideas, products, and services help make communities stronger, more vibrant, and uniquely their own. The bus will travel to key states to drive the debate about what it takes for people, businesses, and communities to thrive. It is planned in partnership with state and local chamber members.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce is the world’s largest business organization representing companies of all sizes across every sector of the economy. Title: New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Article_Text:
New laws trigger a fresh legal fight over Nazi-looted art in Los Angeles and Auschwitz museums
Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
Related video above | Holocaust Survivor Returns to Auschwitz with Family
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of “Adam and Eve.” These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Carnach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death.”
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.
Artworks pit Jewish families against museums
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history. Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.
“These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people,” he said. “It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust.”
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.
“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities,” she said.
New legislation gives lawsuits second wind
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it’s time for museums to “do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history.”
Museums want to preserve paintings for posterity
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, “must remain in the Memorial” to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “ … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”
Advocates hope cases will now be heard on their merit
Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a Philadelphia-area nonprofit that helps Jewish families track down and recover Nazi-looted art, said in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed into law and updated the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently eliminated the expiration date to allow Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely pursue the recovery of these works of art.
Greenberg said the new federal law gave families the right to reclaim their art for up to six years from the time they find out in whose possession they are.
“These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court,” he said. “Every case will be heard on its merits.”
He said the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families have their day in court and a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen art.
“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

Title: FBI at the polls? And another Jan. 6 rioter is up to no good.
Article_Text:
Injustice for All is a weekly series about how the Trump administration is trying to weaponize the justice system—and the people who are fighting back.
This week, we visit with some old friends, talented types like Lindsey Halligan and John Eastman. Also? FBI Director Kash Patel continues to be one of the dumbest guys in the administration.
Oh hello, Lindsey Halligan. What are you doing here?
You might have forgotten all about Lindsey, but she’s back, baby. Sort of.
The Department of Justice is still—STILL—trying to revive its failed prosecutions of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. However, those prosecutions were thrown out because the court found that Halligan was never in her job legally and therefore her miraculous attainment of indictments could not stand.
So, to revive those prosecutions requires the DOJ to argue that Halligan was always and forever in her job legally. Arguments before the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals did not go super well for the administration. One judge on the panel, Henry Floyd, basically said that Halligan signing off on the indictment was the same as having any random person roll in and do so: “What’s different with a man on the street?”
The administration’s position here—that Trump can evade the necessity for Senate confirmation by just reappointing an unconfirmed hack like Halligan for infinite 120-day terms—is nonsense, of course. However, we all know full well that this will ultimately end up at the Supreme Court. Then everything will turn on whatever brainworms are chewing on the gray matter of the conservative justices that particular day.
Oh hello, John Eastman. What are you doing here?
John Eastman’s antics would be comical if he weren’t so powerful, so very much at the center of the Trump administration’s efforts to unmake democracy.
The former Clarence Thomas clerk is responsible for both the fake electors scheme and the faux-scholarship underpinning the challenge to birthright citizenship. He is also disbarred in California thanks to his fake elector antics.
But that’s not slowing Eastman down in the least. Because he’s not disbarred in the Third Circuit Court of Appeals, he’s just joined the legal team representing University of Pennsylvania Professor Amy Wax, saying. “In many ways, Penn’s efforts to cancel [Wax] are part of a broader, despicable cancel culture of which my own Cal Bar proceedings are a part.”
LOL. The university has sought to dismiss, er, cancel Wax for things like openly advocating for the United States to have “more whites and fewer non-whites,” saying that Black law students rarely graduate in the top half of their class, that immigrants are dirty, and that women are inferior to men. How dare they seek to deprive the students of such winning insights? Thank god Eastman is here to help make sure Wax can keep imposing her truly breathtaking range of bigotry on law students.
Meanwhile, Eastman is also taking his disbarment all the way to the Supreme Court because how dare anyone force him to follow the ethics rules that bind all other lawyers? Don’t they know who he is?
DOJ ready to lend a helping hand to Trump’s personal attorneys
And why not? There’s no daylight between the DOJ and Trump’s personal attorneys, so it really isn’t a mystery that the official federal government lawyers—who are supposed to represent you and me and the rest of the country—are instead stanning for Trump’s personal lawyers.
You’ll recall that Trump’s personal lawyers were sanctioned for their participation in the slush fund fraud fiasco, when it became clear the whole “case” was just a scam to get Trump money rather than an actual case. Turns out that sort of thing makes courts a bit sad. But we can’t have any consequences for those folks, now can we?
So now, weirdly, the DOJ is trying to appear in the appeal, where Trump, in his personal capacity, is demanding that the sanctions order be stayed. This kinda brings home the whole point that this was a collusive sham. The DOJ is supposed to be the adversary here, and adversaries do not normally hop into appeals to make sure opposing counsel doesn’t get sanctioned for their bad behavior. But this is how we live now.
The FBI may or may not be at the polls
FBI Director Kash Patel is not the brightest bulb in the very dim firmament that is this administration. Despite being an actual factual lawyer who actually factually practiced, he seems unable to read basic statutes. That’s really the only explanation for why he’s saying that sure, he might send federal agents to polling places despite that being categorically, absolutely against the law.
Worse? He seems to have decided to do this on the fly, during a Senate judiciary hearing, because he got sad that a Democrat dared to ask him a question. When Vermont Sen. Peter Welch asked about whether Patel had told Michigan gubernatorial candidate John James there would be an FBI presence at the polls, Patel got huffy: “We have an election crimes community coordinator at all 56 offices. So you bet we’re gonna have them there … for election interference matters.”
Terrific. Can’t wait for the dumbest of jackboots to screw with elections in blue states because Patel is a spineless baby in thrall to Trump’s belief in nonexistent election fraud.
Another pardoned J6er covers himself in glory
Wow, all of the insurrectionists Trump pardoned could not be more deserving or more upstanding, right? So glad these folks got returned to polite society with no consequences for literal treason.
Sure, about one in 16 have been arrested, charged, or convicted since they were pardoned, but if they weren’t pardoned, they couldn’t make important contributions to society like Peter Schwartz.
Mr. Schwartz has made the most of his post-pardon freedom, it appears, most recently by whipping donuts around a truck, then pulling a gun on the truck’s occupants. He did all of this with an invalid license because he refused to undergo a previous DUI examination. While driving and brandishing a weapon, Schwartz was drunk enough to be slurring his words, and a search turned up some Miller Lite and some cocaine, along with the guns.
Thank god this guy gets to live his best life outside the walls while immigrants are deported for no reason at all. Great system we have here.

Title: We are the leaders we've been waiting for
Article_Text:
Trending
We’re now officially in the run-up to the midterm elections, with less than two months to go before Election Day 2026.
The good news is most Americans now understand how bad Donald Trump is. With the exception of Richard 0Nixon, he’s the most unpopular second-term president at this stage in his tenure in the history of polling going back to the 1940s.
On issues where he once was strong -- like the economy, national security and immigration -- Trump is now underwater, with more Americans opposing than supporting his policies.
All the major problems America now faces are entirely self-inflicted by Trump.
Before he was reelected, the United States was not at war with anyone, and oil moved freely through the Persian Gulf. Now, we’re mired in a war in Iran without apparent end, the gulf is blocked and the Red Sea potentially blocked -- sending oil prices soaring. We’ve also strengthened and made more militant Iran’s ruling regime.
Before he was reelected, the U.S. economy was in good shape. The Economist called it “the envy of the world.” Now prices are rising faster than wages, meaning that most Americans are becoming poorer. We’re even in a trade war with our heretofore closest ally, Canada, and Trump is posting insulting memes about Canada and its prime minister on social media.
Before he was reelected, hardworking people in our communities -- many of them neighbors and friends -- felt safe. Now his mass deportations have created trauma and chaos in our communities, including unpredictable arrests, imprisonments, deportations and deaths.
Finally, Americans are seeing this rot. The great sleeping giant of America is awakening.
But I need to warn you against three attitudes I’m picking up among Democrats and progressives that frankly worry me.
The first is complacency. Some people tell me that Democrats are “sure” to take the House and have a “good chance” to take the Senate.
Maybe the betting odds show this, but taking the House is far from a sure thing. As to the Senate, we need to hold all the seats held by Democrats and also flip five additional ones (I say five because Pennsylvania’s John Fetterman may switch to the Republican Party after the midterms, or vote with Republicans).
Moreover, polls are notoriously unreliable, as we’ve painfully learned.
So please do not fall into complacency. It’s far too easy to sit on your hands and expect that we have the votes. Take nothing for granted.
The second attitude I worry about is the opposite: defeatism. Some people tell me Democrats and progressives “don’t stand a chance” because Trump won’t allow it. He’ll stop at nothing. The fix is in. He’s already sowing chaos on mail-in ballots. And what about the $5,000 bribes, and his bonkers request that his followers cheat?
Please don’t fall into defeatism, either. There’s a decent chance we will win both chambers -- if we work hard enough.
The third attitude that worries me is cynicism. Yesterday someone said to me it “doesn’t matter” if Democrats take the House or even the Senate because Trump will just ignore whatever Congress does.
Look, I know how harrowing the last year and a half has been. Many of us were shocked when he was reelected and have been shocked since then at how ignorant and horrific he and his regime have been.
But there’s no excuse for cynicism. If Democrats control the House, they can make life exceedingly difficult for Trump; if they also control the Senate, they could possibly convict him of impeachable offenses.
We are the only people who will rescue us from this nightmare. We are the leaders we've been waiting for. The next seven weeks are crucial.

Title: Denver Barkey hoping to be center of attention for Flyers
Article_Text:
VOORHEES, N.J. – Denver Barkey made the move from wing to center for a couple of Flyers playoff games last year due to an injury to Noah Cates.
All of 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds, Barkey liked it so much and played well enough that he could wind up there when the season gets underway on Sept. 30.
Barkey is quick enough and light enough on his skates to make up for his lack of size. His hockey IQ is through the roof, which can help keep him out of trouble. He played center in junior in London, Ontario, at age 16. So it’s not a completely overwhelming transition.
“It takes a lot of work to be an established NHL centerman,” Barkey said after Saturday’s intrasquad scrimmage at the Flyers Training Center. “One thing I’ve always taken pride in is being a versatile player, someone who can play center or wing.”
Barkey says whatever experience he lacks at center can be made up by studying a lot of video.
“I know the task at hand, what a centerman needs to do in all three zones through the game,” he said. “Having the opportunity to show them I can play center and hold my own is just another opportunity for me. Looking to run away with it.”
A meeting with the coaching staff over the summer laid the groundwork for the potential switch.
The Flyers don’t have a desperate need in the middle. They already have Trevor Zegras, Sean Couturier, Christian Dvorak and Cates at that position.
“They (the coaches) let me know they like how I played at center in those two playoff games,” the 21-year-old Newmarket, Ont. native said. “I wasn’t out of place sort of thing. I worked on things over the summer that are going to help me excel at that position.”
Barkey only posted 17 points in 43 regular-season games last year, but that could change if he finds himself between a couple talented wingers.
One player Barkey is sure to consult with is Couturier, the Flyers captain who is the dean of Philadelphia professional athletes.
“If I continue to stay there (at center), Coots will be a big one,” Barkey said. “Pick the brain of him … Selke (Trophy) winner, someone who knows how to play the game the right way. He plays the offensive side of the puck and the defensive side of the puck very well.
“He’s just a guy you can put out there in any situation and rely on him. I’ll work with him after practice. See if he has some pointers to help me out.”
A lot of NHL centers go around 6-foot-3 and about 200 pounds. Barkey is far from that, but it won’t stop him from achieving his goal once he sets his mind to it. Carolina playoff hero Logan Stankoven (5-foot-8, 165 pounds) is a good example of overcoming a size deficiency
“Over the years you’ve seen more and more guys be able to have a big impact on this league,” Barkey said. “He (Stankoven) is only 5-8, 5-9 and yet he made a huge impact in all three zones. He did a lot of things a lot of people probably didn’t think he could do. He won a lot of puck battles and he wasn’t afraid. That’s someone I try to keep a close eye on. Stature-wise, we’re pretty similar.”
Coach Rick Tocchet believes Barkey has what it takes to make the switch, if that’s the direction the team opts for.
“There’s something there we have to look at,” Tocchet said. “He’s a smart guy. I don’t think he hurts you defensively. So that (move) is something we’re going to have to look into.”

Title: In the pink: Painting the Planet Pink for cancer research, awareness
Article_Text:
Christopher Hughes, of Archbald, stepped up to the starting line at Saturday’s Paint the Planet Pink 5K with a victory already in hand.
Hughes’ real win came not with an especially stellar time or placement on the leaderboard, but in his wife Aliah’s successful battle against breast cancer.
Both came to the Paint the Planet Pink event decked in pink and determined to help raise money and awareness so others can have the benefit of research and treatment that Aliah Hughes believes saved her life.
Diagnosed in 2024 at only 35 years old, Aliah Hughes points out that women seem to be diagnosed younger and younger.
The Paint the Planet Pink events, geared toward fundraising for cancer research, make overcoming the disease possible, she said.
A tradition and a commitment
Paint the Planet Pink graced Scranton’s downtown not simply as an event, but as a tradition—a gathering of friends, families, and survivors united by memories, hope, and a commitment to support breast cancer research.
The series of events is the brainchild of Barbara Sciandra and Qiana Lehman, who organized a three-day fundraiser in 2014. It has since grown into a regional tradition dedicated to raising money for cancer research at the University of Pennsylvania.
Sciandra founded the initiative to support research into an immunotherapy treatment that she credits with saving her life after her 2012 breast cancer diagnosis.
In 2024, the organization introduced a new logo and rebranded to Paint the Planet Pink, moving its 5K race, walk, and Gentlemen’s Dash to Scranton. Despite the shift, Sciandra emphasizes that multiple events remain anchored in Luzerne County, backed by strong regional support.
Over its first 12 years, the effort raised $1 million for cancer research at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. Yet as Sciandra looked out on a sea of pink Saturday, what she saw most vividly were the faces—returning supporters who have attended since day one alongside new faces eager to learn about breast cancer research and to contribute.
Balancing event preparation with a busy home life isn’t easy, especially as her three children grow toward adulthood and take on numerous activities. But Sciandra stays driven by her deep commitment to her family and to others facing cancer.
Running like men – in heels
The Gentlemen’s Dash is the brainchild of Barbara Sciandra’s husband, Sal.
After the event’s first season in 2014, the couple was discussing ideas for future fundraising events. Sal came up with the idea of men in high heels racing down Main Street. He believed that his idea would serve as a symbol of the pain that women, and even men, face while undergoing cancer treatment.
Now, it is a top fundraiser and a favorite of those attending the event. Sciandra remembers back to the event’s inaugural season, when she called Ed Ackerman and asked him if he would participate.
Ackerman didn’t really know what he was agreeing to, but simply said a quick, “yes.”
He got to run in flats that year, she said, laughing.
Russell Keeler also ran in that first Gentlemen’s Dash and was back to give it another try Saturday.
He purchased his size 15 high heels on Amazon, with a thicker heel he hoped would provide a little stability to his steps.
Keeler’s goal wasn’t to finish first, but to simply make it down the street without falling, he said.
The real win, he said, was the fundraising the event provides. The window for voting for a favorite dasher runs until Oct. 3.
Upcoming events
Although the 5K, family run and Gentlemen’s Dash are among the best-known events of the Paint the Planet Pink effort, the fun and fundraising aren’t over yet.
On the schedule are a cash and purse bingo on Sunday, Sept. 27, at St. Maria Goretti Church Banquet Hall in Laflin; ’90s trivia night and meat raffle on Tuesday, Sept. 29, at Sabatini’s Bottleshop in Exeter; and Paint the Red Mill Pink, a guest bartender happy hour, on Saturday, Oct. 3, at the Red Mill in Pittston.
Details, tickets, and donation options are available at painttheplanetpink.org.

Title: Chuseok festival in Blue Bell celebrates Korean culture's growing global influence
Article_Text:
Korean culture’s global rise takes center stage at Chuseok festival in Blue Bell
Hundreds joined together at Montgomery County Community College in Blue Bell for “Happy Chuseok Fest 2026.”
Ask Pastor Daniel Cho why Korean culture has become so popular in the United States, and he just smiles, shaking his head in wonderment.
“I’m not sure, but we’re pleasantly shocked,” said Cho, 59, a Montgomery County Presbyterian minister, who is leaving soon for missionary work in Vietnam. “Turn on the TV and see Korean dramas, K-pop music, and Korean food being everywhere.
“It’s wonderful how we’ve gotten to share our culture. When someone loves what you love, it’s exciting.”
That excitement was palpable Saturday at Montgomery County Community College in Blue Bell, where about 1,500 people gathered for “Happy Chuseok Fest 2026,” a Korean Thanksgiving celebration.
Part of a 2,000-year-old tradition, Chuseok is the time Koreans pause to reflect on family, gratitude, ancestors, harvest, and respect for nature.
“I love it because I get to spend time with my family,” said Kelsey Chung, 14, a ninth grader from Newtown Square. “It’s important to remember the traditions.”
Sponsored by the Korean Culture Community Foundation and Montgomery County, the Chuseok festival is highly significant for the roughly 30,000 to 40,000 Korean Americans living in Pennsylvania, said Sharon Hartz, president of the foundation.
“We know Christian and Jewish holidays,” she said. “But Koreans didn’t really have a holiday that was theirs. Chuseok is becoming more widely known.”
At the festival, vendors were selling kimchi (fermented cabbage), kimbap (rice, vegetables, and meat in seaweed), bulgogi (marinated beef), and, of course, fried chicken, the most popular Korean food abroad, according to the Korea Herald.
Beyond chicken, Korea is widely known for a “deep-rooted culture that people around the world have grabbed onto,” said sociologist Sam Richards of Pennsylvania State University, a Korean scholar who spoke at Saturday’s event.
“South Korea was poor 60 years ago, but it’s an economic superpower now,” said Richards, described by the Korea Times as a “megastar” whose YouTube videos are popular in Korea because of his love for and understanding of the culture.
“The Korean government rebuilt the country by putting money into exporting culture — music, television, movies.”
Americans, he said, are quite familiar with the K-pop superstars BTS, the most popular band in the world. Then, among other works, there is Squid Game, the dystopian thriller TV series, as well as the black-comedy film Parasite, Richards said.
“The government succeeded, as people were attracted to what South Korea has exported.”
A key to the appeal of Korean entertainment is that humility, a national trait, stands out among actors and musical artists, Richards said. Also, he noted, “you won’t see Korean artists putting themselves forward.”
“Pop stars say ‘we,’ not ‘I,’” Richards said.
Korea’s new role in the American zeitgeist is remarkable, said Nani Shin, executive director of the Philadelphia Asian American Film Foundation, whose organization was tabling at the Chuseok event.
“No one in the 1970s knew where Korea was,” Shin, who was born in South Korea, said. “Now, the culture isn’t only known, but celebrated. It’s wild.”
It is important to remember, however, that Koreans look to keep their traditions alive for themselves and their children.
“That’s why I’m here,” said Will Press, 43, who stood outside the event Saturday. He married a Korean woman, he said, which means “she, and I, want our children to know that Korea is part of their heritage.”

Title: Trump says some routine immunizations will be split into 5 shots
Article_Text:
Trump says some routine immunizations will be split into 5 shots. Vaccine experts say it won’t work
President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration is planning to recommend that certain childhood immunizations be broken up into five separate shots, each with a “small amount of the vaccine.” These “20% doses” would each be given six months apart, he said.
Related video above: Flu and COVID-19 vaccines are rolling out, but one shot is still not available
“Instead of a child going in and having a tremendous amount of different vaccines pumped into a big proportion of the body … we’re going to recommend that they do five doses marked one, two, three, four, five and that they be given in six-month intervals, so that a small amount of the vaccine gets pumped into the body,” Trump said.
Such a plan would render vaccines ineffective and would not make them safer, said Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.
Trump also said Friday that “certain vaccines were taken out because they’re not needed until the child would be much older,” an apparent reference to the federal childhood vaccine schedule — which the administration attempted to overhaul this year before it was temporarily blocked by a federal judge.
It’s unclear which vaccines Trump was referring to at Friday’s news conference; he specifically mentioned only the polio vaccine, which he said has “been amazing.”
Trump suggested that the federal vaccination schedule changes he referenced Friday would lead to a “massive reduction in autism,” even though extensive scientific studies of vaccines have yielded no evidence of a connection to autism.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for further details about the plans that Trump outlined Friday.
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — who was standing by Trump as he outlined the planned vaccine changes — received a standing ovation Thursday at the conference of the anti-vaccine advocacy group Children’s Health Defense, where he gave the keynote. He praised Trump’s embrace of vaccine skeptics, telling the conference attendees, “You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” and saying he would “stay in this fight.”
In August, Trump signed an executive order aimed at reshaping the federal government’s approach toward childhood vaccines, insisting that infants should receive fewer immunizations over a longer period and advising that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine be separated into three individual shots, despite little scientific evidence supporting such sweeping changes.
Trump has previously claimed that “large amounts – like vats of vaccine – are currently pumped into your child’s body” and that this supposedly large volume of fluid – “the size of a bottle of soda” – was dangerous.
The standard dose of MMR vaccine given to children around 12 months of age is 0.5 milliliters, or CCs, about one-tenth of a teaspoon.
Trump’s idea to split up the shots “is buffoonery,” said Offit, a vaccine inventor. He noted that vaccines are studied extensively so their dosing schedule is optimized for efficacy and safety, and he said that reducing the amount administered and giving more shots would make it so the vaccines do not work while doing nothing to increase safety.
“When you create a vaccine, you do a dose-response curve, and you’re trying to give the least amount of vaccine that induces an immune response that’s protective. So you don’t want to give too much, where you know you don’t need all that, and you don’t want to give too little, where it’s, you know, sub-immunogenic,” meaning it wouldn’t induce an immune response. Put more simply, Offit told CNN, “What he’s suggesting would not work. He’s basically saying he wants to give vaccines in a manner in which they wouldn’t be protective.”
Offit also pointed out that vaccines do not overwhelm babies’ immune systems, as they expose us to much less than we encounter every day naturally.
“You make a billion new B and T cells every day to handle the onslaught of viruses and bacteria from your environment,” Offit said. “Vaccines are literally a drop in the ocean of what you encounter and manage every day.
“The notion that vaccines in any way are overwhelming your immune system, causing chronic disease, is just fanciful.”
CNN’s Tami Luhby, Brenda Goodman and Jen Christensen contributed to this report.

Title: 100 years ago in Redlands: Crowd gathers at Redlands Bowl to hear radio broadcast of Dempsey-Tunney fight
Article_Text:
Sept. 20, 1926
Facts to present Dempsey-Tunney fight news
With the co-operation of Arthur Munzig of the Munzig Radio Shop The Facts invites all interested to come to the Amphitheater Thursday evening to listen in on the Dempsey-Tunney fight, beginning about 6 o’clock. Reception will be over KHJ, the Los Angeles Times having made arrangements to broadcast details of the contest.
For this event Mr. Munzig will use a Grebe Syncrophase set, presenting an opportunity for radio owners and prospective purchasers to get a demonstration of this particular type of radio. Loud speakers will be placed at points of vantage, so there will be no difficulty in getting all of the news concerning the fight.
All are invited. You will be the guests of Mr. Munzig and The Facts.
Sept. 23, 1926
Redlands to get returns of fight by radio
Many Redlands people will be A.W.O.L. this evening at the time of the big Dempsey-Tunney battle in Philadelphia. For while their bodies will be at the amphitheater here listening to the returns relayed by the Facts through the courtesy of Munzig Radio Shop and the Grebe Syncrophase, their souls will be gathered around the ringside in the Sesqui-Centennial city.
And as the announcer tells off the fight, blow by blow, those fans will hear the thud of the padded gloves on the perfect bodies of the two fighters, and their nostrils will be filled with the battle. It is going to be a great fight, no mistake about that.
The big fight will be on about 5:45 Redlands time, as near as can be ascertained. It is supposed to start at 8:45 Eastern Standard Time, which is about 9:45 Philadelphia time under daylight saving. That makes it about 5:45 in Redlands. Before that time there will be preliminaries to entertain the big crowd.
Redlands has a financial interest in the fight, at least some folks have. For cigars, fountain drinks, and in some cases, a few dollars have been wagered on the outcome. And all through the business section there are pools, the winner to be decided by knockout, number of rounds and other things.
Sept. 24, 1926
Radio report of fight was heard by large crowd
The Dempsey-Tunney fight was relayed to a large audience yesterday evening by the Munzig Radio Company at the amphitheater. Mr. Munzig used a standard Grebe Syncrophase set with two Baldwin loud speakers, connected in series.
Mr. Munzig tuned in on KHJ, the Los Angeles Times, at 4:30 and the listeners were given a program of music from the main studio of KHJ. At 5:15 the microphone was moved into the Associated Press room and preliminary bout results were announced. There was a slight echo in the reproduction, caused by the walls of the Associated Press room at KHJ, but this was soon cut out by Mr. Munzig, using the patented color tone on the Grebe Syncrophase, and the reception was clear and distinct throughout the entire program.
The results were broadcast blow for blow from round one to and including round nine, then came the sudden announcement that “Tunney wins,” and it was almost like being at the ringside, as the listeners rose to their feet and cheered.
The Munzig Radio Company has received many cards of thanks in regard to the program, and takes this opportunity to tell the public that it was a real pleasure to make the relay to them and that they are grateful for the appreciation shown.
Editor’s note: It appears that Arthur L. Munzig took up dealing in radio sets in Redlands in the mid-1920s, only a few years after that new technology became available to the general public. His Munzig Radio Co. is listed in the 1927 Redlands city directory as an authorized dealer of Kolster-Grebe-Crosley Radio, at 9 E. Citrus Ave.
Before that, when the 1925 directory was compiled, he and Roy T. Herold were involved in manufacturing radio equipment and sets with their Ray-Dee-Artcraft Manufacturing Co. that had an office at 12 E. Central Ave. and factory at 1005-17 Tribune St.
Munzig is listed in the 1923 directory as an electrician, a good background for working with 1920s radio sets, and he had returned to that work when the 1929 directory was compiled.
It’s not clear when or how long he went back to radio, but Redlands’ December 1945 telephone directory has a listing for Munzig, Arthur L., Radio Sales & Service, at 19 Fifth St. That was 19 years after the 1926 Jack Dempsey-Gene Tunney fight and a few months after the end of World War II, when both radio sets and the world had undergone great changes since the 1920s.
Speaking of changes, note that Redlands, probably all of California, was not on daylight saving time in 1926. If it had been, 9:45 p.m. Philadelphia time under daylight saving would have been 6:45 p.m. in Redlands, not 5:45.
Articles are from the Redlands Daily Facts archive and are presented as they were written at the time.

Title: Every act on Ed Sheeran's tour has quit. His next show is tomorrow.
Article_Text:
Every act on Ed Sheeran's tour has quit. His next show is tomorrow.
The British singer has 10 U.S. performances left — and no one to open them.
Ed Sheeran will take the stage Saturday night at Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field for the first show of his Loop Tour since Macklemore was dropped, likely performing solo after all of his remaining opening acts and his backing band quit in solidarity with the rapper over his removal from the tour for pro-Palestinian comments.
Hours after Sheeran released a statement saying it was the promoter's decision to remove Macklemore from the tour and not his, the rest of his supporting acts — Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Danish pop band Lukas Graham and songwriter Finneas — as well as Sheeran's house band, Beoga, announced that they were pulling out in protest.
"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas, the brother of Billie Eilish, wrote in a note posted to Instagram. "I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people."
The Irish artists cited their country's history of oppression in their decisions to drop out.
"I don't take the decision lightly. Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this," Rowe wrote in his own Instagram post. "But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children."
"We are Irish people who understand colonialism," Beoga said in a statement on Instagram. "As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be."
Finneas was scheduled to be the supporting act for stops in Chile, Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil.
Rowe and Lukas Graham had been due to open for Sheeran on his remaining 11 North American tour dates.
Sheeran is scheduled to take the stage Saturday night at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, marking the first Loop Tour show since Macklemore's removal. The concert was pushed back from 5:30 p.m. to 8 p.m. ET after the openers dropped out, according to Ticketmaster. Music industry sources told TMZ that Sheeran is prepared to perform solo, without his backing band. He has not commented publicly since Tuesday.
What to expect Saturday
A coalition of pro-Palestinian groups plans to rally outside Lincoln Financial Field at 4:30 p.m. Saturday. Speakers will include representatives from Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott Cooknsolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann, according to a statement.
Philadelphia Police Department spokesperson Tanya Little said in a statement that the department "is working closely with venue and event organizers to help ensure the safety of concert attendees, employees, and neighborhood residents."
Resale prices for Saturday's show have fallen sharply. TickPick data cited by Forbes showed the cheapest ticket at $51 on Friday morning, down from $100 on Tuesday. By Friday afternoon, StubHub listings had dropped to as low as $42.
Remaining dates of Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour
- Sept. 19: Lincoln Financial Field, Philadelphia
- Sept. 25-26: Gillette Stadium, Foxborough, Mass.
- Oct. 3: Mercedes-Benz Stadium, Atlanta
- Oct. 10: Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis
- Oct. 17: Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C.
- Oct. 24: AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas
- Oct 29-30: Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino, Hollywood, Fla.
- Nov 7: Raymond James Stadium, Tampa
- Nov. 21-22: Estadio Bicentenario De La Florida, Santiago, Chile
- Nov. 26: Nueva Olla Stadium, Asunción, Paraguay
- Nov. 29: Tomás Adolfo Ducó Stadium (Huracán Stadium), Buenos Aires, Argentina
- Dec. 5-6: Nubank Parque, Sao Paulo
- Dec. 11: Estadio Ciudad de los Deportes, Mexico City
None of the U.S. shows are sold out.
It's unclear whether ticket holders can exchange their tickets or get a refund following the lineup changes.
According to Ticketmaster, event organizers determine refund policies, and they are "only allowed in limited circumstances."
Ticketmaster's standard purchase policy states: "Opening Acts are subject to change or cancellation at any time without notice. No refund will be given due to a change in or cancellation of a Participant or Opening Act."
And according to Sheeran's website, all sales are final: "If you change your mind about your ticket purchase, you are not entitled to a refund or exchange on your ticket purchase."
The Philadelphia news site Billy Penn reported that some ticket holders said Lincoln Financial Field has begun issuing refunds due to the lineup change.
How we got here
Earlier this month, Macklemore performed as Sheeran's opening act at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he made pro-Palestinian comments and performed his protest song "Hind's Hall."
The song was written after protests in support of Palestine occurred on college campuses across the U.S. in 2024, and is named after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl who was killed by Israeli troops in Gaza. Last month, Israel's military acknowledged that its troops had opened fire on the car carrying Hind and her family and said it had opened a criminal investigation into the killing.
"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine,'" Macklemore said onstage at MetLife Stadium.
"To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you," the rapper added.
His comments drew criticism from pop singer Pink and pro-Israel groups, including the Israeli-American Council, which started a petition to have the Grammy-winning artist dropped from the tour.
Robert Kraft, owner of the NFL's New England Patriots, said in a statement on Monday that Macklemore wouldn't be welcome at Gillette Stadium for the tour's scheduled performances at the end of September.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Carolina Panthers and Atlanta Falcons owners also decided not to host the tour if Macklemore remained on the bill, and that Philadelphia Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie was reaching the same conclusion before the rapper was dropped.
According to Macklemore, Kraft — who in 2024 withdrew funding for Columbia University over its handling of protests against Israel's war in Gaza — had "rallied some of the other stadium owners" to give Sheeran "an ultimatum: If Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play."
In his statement, Sheeran said that he had spoken with Kraft and the other venues "to try and build a bridge," but that their "decision was final."
"After Macklemore's performances at my New Jersey shows, venues on my upcoming tour dates communicated that they would pull the shows if he was still supporting," he said on Instagram Tuesday. "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine."
The promoter, Messina Touring Group, said in a statement to Rolling Stone that it had been notified by venues on Sheeran's upcoming U.S. tour that they would "not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
The company said that "after discussions with stakeholders," it decided to remove Macklemore.
Representatives for the Messina Touring Group did not immediately return a request for comment.
In his Instagram post, Sheeran also insisted that "I do not use my professional platform for politics."
"My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds," he said.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum."
But several commenters were quick to point out that Sheeran has, in fact, used his professional platform to support political causes, including a video he posted ahead of his performance at a 2022 benefit concert for Ukraine.
"I just wanted to say to all Ukrainians, I love you, I stand with you, and I'm so proud to be playing this fundraising event," he said.
On Wednesday, Macklemore pledged to donate $1 million from the net earnings he received from Sheeran's tour to organizations that support Palestinians. The rapper then called on Kraft to match his donation.
Within hours, Kraft issued his own statement, saying, "I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting. Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis."
Kraft added: "I'd like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships."
Kraft's $2 million and Sheeran's matching contribution will go to the Palestinian Children's Relief Fund, Heal Palestine, the Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, the U.N. Relief and Works Agency and Anera, according to the Associated Press.

Title: Ed Sheeran to resume tour after acts withdraw over Macklemore comments
Article_Text:
Ed Sheeran to resume tour after acts withdraw over Macklemore comments
PHILADELPHIA - Ed Sheeran is expected to resume his tour Saturday, potentially without supporting acts, after they withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped following pro-Palestinian comments made onstage.
Dig deeper:
It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original U.S. opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.
Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.
RELATED: 4 acts drop out of Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with rapper Macklemore
Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday's show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organizations plans to protest outside the show Saturday afternoon.
The backstory:
The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming "Free Palestine" during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday.
Within hours of Sheeran's statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.
RELATED: Finneas drops out of Ed Sheeran tour
Macklemore said Wednesday he is donating $1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran's representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment.
Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No. 3 top-earning concert act since 2021.
Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.
What they're saying:
The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.
He also said he "spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge" before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.
The Source: The Associated Press contributed to this report. The information came from statements by Ed Sheeran and Macklemore, comments from representatives for Robert Kraft, concert ticket and tour information, Pollstar’s concert industry data, and reporting on the planned protest by pro-Palestinian organizations. This story was reported from Los Angeles.
